Project Proposal: Permitless Concealed Carry and Firearm Mortality

Jingyi Wang

2026-11-18

Source: vignettes/proposal.qmd

To: BST260 Teaching Team, Fall 2026
From: Jingyi Wang
Repository: https://github.com/JingyiWang6/finalproject
Project website: https://jingyiwang6.github.io/finalproject/

Research question and objectives

Among the 50 U.S. states during 2014–2024, is allowing permitless concealed carry associated with changes in the annual age-adjusted firearm mortality rate?

What interests me most is how states differ from one another. I do not want to start by assuming that permitless concealed carry is a good or bad policy. Instead, I want to see whether states show similar patterns or whether a group average hides quite different experiences.

I plan to use the RAND legislation data (gunleg) and CDC firearm mortality data (cdcfiremort) already provided in the course. The project will start with two questions: when did states change their concealed-carry rules, and what was happening to mortality in those states around the same time? The aim is to describe the patterns and assess an association, without assuming in advance that the policy raises or lowers mortality.

Reasoning behind the scope

One design choice is to focus on a single policy rather than count all firearm laws. A state with more entries in the RAND file is not necessarily more restrictive: entries can represent different policies, amendments, or replacements. Focusing on permitless concealed carry gives the project a clearer comparison, although the legal details will still need checking.

A simple comparison of states with and without this policy would be easy to plot, but difficult to interpret. The states may already have had different mortality rates before adoption. For that reason, the analysis will also show each state’s own trajectory, including the years before its policy changed. Similar group averages could hide states moving in opposite directions. If the trends were already moving apart before adoption, that would also change how I interpret a later difference between the groups.

There is also a tradeoff in choosing the outcome. Overall firearm mortality is available in the course data, but it combines deaths with different intents. A pattern in this outcome would not, by itself, explain what happened to firearm homicide. That limits the question this project can answer.

Data sources, population, and feasibility

The population of interest is residents of the 50 U.S. states. The main unit of analysis will be a state–calendar year; individual legislation records will be the starting unit for the policy-data vignette.

Dataset Original source and provenance Role in the project
gunleg RAND State Firearm Law Database and supporting documentation; distributed in the course template and retained in finalproject Identify concealed-carry policy categories, effective dates, supersession dates, and relevant statutory notes
cdcfiremort CDC/NCHS Stats of the States: Firearm Mortality, based on National Vital Statistics System mortality data; distributed in the course template and retained in finalproject Annual state firearm death counts and age-adjusted death rates

A preliminary structural check of the bundled data found 1,902 legislation records and 612 mortality records. The mortality file contains 51 jurisdictions for 2005 and each year from 2014 through 2024. I will restrict the main analysis to the continuous 2014–2024 period and exclude the District of Columbia, giving at most 550 state–years before policy-coding exclusions. I will not interpolate the missing 2006–2013 period. These checks establish feasibility; they are not findings about the research question.

The analysis will use the bundled snapshots. The final vignettes will document the original source links, package version, repository commit, file checksums, access date, and cleaning decisions. I will also check which RAND database version the bundled extract represents; the version on its current webpage may differ.

Variables and data preparation

Exposure: a binary indicator of permitless concealed-carry policy, based on the Law.Class category carrying a concealed weapon (ccw) and the Law.Class.Subtype label shall issue (permit not required). I will inspect Content, Effective.Date.Note, effective-date fields, and supersession fields to check coverage and resolve overlapping records. This measures the RAND policy category, not unrestricted firearm carrying by every resident.

For the primary coding, a state–year will be exposed (1) only when a verified qualifying policy covers the entire calendar year. A verified year before adoption will be coded 0. Years containing a policy transition will be excluded from the primary comparison. For example, a policy introduced in July should not make the preceding six months count as exposed. This choice sacrifices some observations but makes the annual groups easier to interpret. Unresolved histories or ambiguous dates will be coded missing, not automatically treated as unexposed. Absence of a qualifying record alone will not establish policy absence. A sensitivity analysis will use year-end policy status when dates permit reliable classification.

Outcome: Death.Rate, a continuous age-adjusted firearm mortality rate per 100,000 population. Deaths. will provide descriptive counts. The counts and age-adjusted rates will be kept separate; dividing one by the other would not give a valid population denominator.

I will standardize state identifiers, check uniqueness of state–year keys, and join the two datasets by state and year. Missing or suppressed outcomes will remain missing. I will tabulate missingness, unmatched records, and exclusions, without imputing policy histories or mortality rates.

Two planned analysis vignettes

1. Concealed-carry policy changes across states

vignettes/policy-history.qmd will analyze gunleg. It will document the source and coding rules, summarize law classes and date completeness, and describe variation in concealed-carry policy histories. Planned outputs include a table of adoption years, annual numbers of states in each verified policy category, and a state-by-year policy timeline. Reusable R functions will convert validated policy histories into state–year indicators and flag uncertain records. It will also report how many state–years cannot be confidently classified, so the final comparison does not hide uncertainty in the policy data.

2. Firearm mortality trends and policy associations

vignettes/firearm-mortality.qmd will analyze cdcfiremort and link it to the policy indicators. It will report mortality distributions, state-specific changes, and the number of observed state–years by exposure group. Planned figures include state trend lines, a state-by-year mortality heatmap, and descriptive comparisons by policy status. Unweighted summaries across states will be labeled as state-level summaries, not national population mortality rates.

Descriptive plots and tables will be the main results. If enough states have usable observations before and after a policy change, I will also try an exploratory linear model with policy status, state fixed effects, and calendar-year fixed effects. The report will give the coefficient in deaths per 100,000, a confidence interval using standard errors clustered by state, and the number of states and policy changes contributing to it. A complicated model would not be useful if most of the comparison depended on only a few states; in that case, the report will explain why the descriptive results are more informative.

Confounding, sensitivity analyses, and limitations

The adjustment priorities are longstanding differences between states and changes affecting the country in the same year. These motivate the state and year fixed effects, chosen before examining the exposure–outcome association. Age adjustment is already part of the CDC outcome. Poverty, urbanization, firearm ownership, other policies, and state-specific pandemic impacts could still change over time and confound the comparison. The two datasets do not measure these adequately, so the report will state that they remain unadjusted.

Sensitivity analyses will compare full-year and year-end exposure coding, omit 2020–2021, and examine whether conclusions depend heavily on any one state. I will distinguish planned analyses from any exploratory additions and report unstable or null associations.

Policy adoption is not random. Staggered adoption, potentially different effects across states and time, short follow-up for recent adopters, policy exceptions, and uncertain dates limit interpretation of a pooled fixed-effects coefficient. Overall firearm mortality also combines different intents, potentially masking different patterns. These are aggregate data, so state-level associations cannot establish individual risk or a policy’s causal effect. Findings and limitations will be reported together in each analysis vignette.

Deliverables and workflow

The final deliverable will be a valid R package and public pkgdown website with the two analysis vignettes, documented helper functions, reproducible tables and figures, and R session information. Work will proceed from data checks to descriptive analysis, followed by the exploratory model only if the data support it. The README will introduce the project and link to the reports. These are plans for the final project; the policy–mortality analyses have not yet been completed.
